newsitem.title: NORWAY: Nobel winner Belo talks peace, snubs politics. [CORRECTED 13:54 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Nobel winner Belo talks peace, snubs politics. [CORRECTED 13:54 GMT]

text.p: East Timorese Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo, co-winner of the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize, has brought a message of peace and reconciliation to Oslo and deftly avoided political comment on the situation in his troubled homeland.
"I am a religious leader. Leave the political issues to the politicians, please," Belo told a news conference on Monday, a day before the award ceremony in the Norwegian capital.
"As a religious leader, I am ready to collaborate with everybody who are really committed to efforts for peace and justice in East Timor," the bishop said.

Belo was awarded the prestigious prize along with self-exiled resistance leader Jose Ramos Horta for their efforts to find a peaceful end to the conflict in the former Portuguese colony, which has been in turmoil since Indonesia invaded it in 1975.

The bishop, who has defended his parishioners against human rights violations by the Indonesian military, has walked a tightrope between the territory's Jakarta-appointed government and his frustrated people.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas last month warned Belo against meddling in politics after an interview in which the German magazine Der Spiegel quoted him as saying Indonesian troops treated East Timorese like "scabby dogs" and "slaves".
Belo denied the remarks, saying he was misquoted.
Thousands of youths linked to Indonesia's ruling Golkar party protested outside Jakarta's parliament and demanded a public apology from Belo, who was then in Jakarta.

The public criticism of Belo angered East Timorese and sparked protests in his defence by students in the provincial capital of Dili. More than 60,000 people gathered to welcome the bishop home on his return from the Indonesian capital.
The fiery, often outspoken priest was saying mass in a school in East Timor's capital, Dili, when the announcement was made that he and Ramos Horta had shared the 1996 prize.
Belo, born in Baucau, East Timor, in February 1948 (corrects year), was ordained in July 1980 in Lisbon and returned a year later to take up a teaching position in his home town.
It is said that it was during this period that he developed a close affinity to the youth of East Timor who now are in the vanguard of anti-Jakarta dissidence and won their respect.
He was appointed apostolic administrator of the diocese of the East Timor capital of Dili, in May 1983.
While he has often spoken out against Indonesia's sometimes harsh rule in East Timor, Belo has equally called for the restless youth in the territory to stop fighting.
Indonesian security officials regularly call him to the scene of disputes by to help to calm unrest, while his seaside residence in Dili is often used as a refuge.

Belo's presence as an observer at U.N.-sponsored talks between long-time warring East Timorese factions proved crucial in the first dialogue, held in Austria in June, 1995, to include all the various parties.

The talks, part of two U.N. initiatives to solve the problems surrounding East Timor's status, were the first meetings between pro- and anti-integration groups in exile since Indonesia's invasion of the territory.
